nodes.label: Laplacian of a Scalar Field
nodes.explanation: Defines the Laplacian as the divergence of the gradient, ∇²f = ∇·(∇f), gives its Cartesian component form as a sum of second partials, and covers linearity, worked examples (polynomials, r², 1/r away from the origin), harmonic functions (∇²f=0), and the operator's role in Laplace's/the heat equation. Does not cover the vector Laplacian, curvilinear-coordinate forms, or the distributional behavior of ∇²(1/r) at the origin — those belong to other nodes.
nodes.content:
Imagine a thin metal plate whose temperature has settled into a steady pattern that no longer changes with time. Heat is still moving inside the plate — flowing from hot regions toward cold ones — but at every interior point the flow in exactly balances the flow out, so the temperature at that point stays fixed forever. Now pick a single interior point and ask a sharper question: is this point systematically hotter or colder than the average of the temperatures immediately surrounding it? A thermometer placed at the point only reports the value there; it says nothing about how that value compares to its neighborhood. What is needed is a way to measure, at a single point, whether a scalar field bulges upward or dips downward relative to its surroundings in every direction at once — not just along one line, but throughout three-dimensional space. That measurement is the Laplacian of a scalar field.

=== SECTION 1: The Divergence of the Gradient ===

A scalar field \( f(x,y,z) \) has a gradient \( \nabla f \), a vector field whose value at each point is the direction and rate of steepest increase of \( f \) there. A vector field \( \mathbf{F} \) has a divergence \( \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} \), a scalar at each point measuring the net outward flux per unit volume — how much the vector field is spreading out from that point versus collapsing into it.

These two operations compose naturally: feed the gradient vector field \( \nabla f \) into the divergence, and ask whether \( \nabla f \) is spreading outward or collapsing inward around a point. If \( \nabla f \) collapses inward at a point, it means the rate of increase of \( f \) is shrinking as you move outward in every direction — which happens precisely when \( f \) itself bulges upward there, like the peak of a hill, so that \( f \) is larger at the point than the nearby average. If \( \nabla f \) spreads outward, \( f \) dips downward, like the bottom of a bowl, and is smaller at the point than the nearby average. This is exactly the comparison the opening problem asked for, and it is why the Laplacian is defined as the divergence of the gradient, not some other combination:
\[ \nabla^2 f \;=\; \nabla \cdot (\nabla f). \]
The reverse composition, "gradient of the divergence," is not even available here, since divergence takes a vector field as input and \( f \) is a scalar; only \( \nabla \cdot (\nabla f) \) type-checks, and it is exactly this one that carries the concavity meaning above.

This matches a familiar single-variable fact: for a function \( f(x) \) of one variable, \( f''(x) > 0 \) means \( f \) is concave up (a local dip relative to its neighbors) and \( f''(x) < 0 \) means concave down (a local bulge). The Laplacian generalizes this by checking concavity along every direction through a point simultaneously and adding the results together. This one-variable picture is a useful quick intuition to keep alongside the divergence-of-gradient definition; the two are consistent, not competing, descriptions of the same object.

To turn the definition into something computable, write out both operations in Cartesian coordinates. The gradient has components
\[ \nabla f = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \right), \]
and the divergence of a vector field \( \mathbf{F} = (F_1, F_2, F_3) \) is
\[ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_3}{\partial z}. \]
Substituting \( \mathbf{F} = \nabla f \), so that \( F_1 = \partial f/\partial x \), \( F_2 = \partial f/\partial y \), \( F_3 = \partial f/\partial z \), gives
\[ \nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\!\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial z}\right) = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2}. \]
This sum of unmixed second partial derivatives is the Cartesian component form of the Laplacian, and it is the form almost all hands-on computation uses. (The symbol \( \Delta f \) is also common notation for the same object; this document sticks to \( \nabla^2 f \).)

[QUESTION 1]
Let \( f(x,y,z) = x^2y + y^2z + z^2x \). Compute \( \nabla^2 f \) at the point \( (1,2,3) \).

(A) 6
(B) 8
(C) 10
(D) 12
(E) 14
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 2: Linearity of the Laplacian ===

Both operations that make up the Laplacian are linear. Differentiation is linear, so for constants \( a, b \) and scalar fields \( f, g \),
\[ \nabla(af + bg) = a\nabla f + b \nabla g, \]
since each component of the gradient is just a partial derivative of \( af+bg \), and partial differentiation distributes over sums and pulls out constants. Divergence is linear for the same reason: it is built entirely out of partial derivatives of the components of a vector field, so
\[ \nabla \cdot (a\mathbf{F} + b\mathbf{G}) = a\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} + b\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{G}. \]
Composing two linear operations gives a linear operation, so
\[ \nabla^2(af+bg) = a\nabla^2 f + b \nabla^2 g. \]
The same conclusion falls straight out of the Cartesian component form: \( \nabla^2 \) is a sum of second partial derivatives, and second partial differentiation is linear at each term, so the sum inherits linearity termwise. This property will do real work later — it means the Laplacian of a complicated field can often be built from the Laplacians of simpler pieces rather than recomputed from scratch.

[QUESTION 2]
Suppose at some point \( P \), \( \nabla^2 f(P) = 5 \) and \( \nabla^2 g(P) = -3 \). Using linearity, what is \( \nabla^2(4f - 2g) \) at \( P \)?

(A) 14
(B) 18
(C) 20
(D) 23
(E) 26
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 3: Radial Functions — \( r^2 \) and \( 1/r \) Away From the Origin ===

Let \( r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2} \) denote distance from the origin, so \( r^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2 \). Its Laplacian is a direct computation: \( \partial(r^2)/\partial x = 2x \), so \( \partial^2(r^2)/\partial x^2 = 2 \), and likewise for \( y \) and \( z \). Summing,
\[ \nabla^2(r^2) = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, \]
a constant, the same at every point of space.

Many other radial functions of interest are powers of \( r \), and it is worth handling them all at once rather than one at a time. For \( r \neq 0 \), the chain rule gives \( \partial r/\partial x = x/r \) (since \( r = (x^2+y^2+z^2)^{1/2} \)), so for \( f = r^n \),
\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(r^n) = n r^{n-1}\frac{\partial r}{\partial x} = n x\, r^{n-2}. \]
Differentiating again, using the product rule on \( x \) and \( r^{n-2} \), and the chain rule once more on \( r^{n-2} \):
\[ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}(r^n) = n\!\left[(n-2)x^2 r^{n-4} + r^{n-2}\right]. \]
The \( y \) and \( z \) second partials are identical with \( y^2 \) or \( z^2 \) in place of \( x^2 \). Summing all three and using \( x^2+y^2+z^2 = r^2 \),
\[ \nabla^2(r^n) = n(n-2)\,r^{n-4}(x^2+y^2+z^2) + 3n\,r^{n-2} = n(n-2)\,r^{n-2} + 3n\,r^{n-2} = n(n+1)\,r^{n-2}, \]
valid for \( r \neq 0 \). As a check, setting \( n=2 \) gives \( 2\cdot 3\, r^0 = 6 \), matching the direct computation above exactly — the general formula reduces correctly to the special case already worked out by hand.

[QUESTION 3]
Using \( \nabla^2(r^n) = n(n+1)\,r^{n-2} \) for \( r \neq 0 \), evaluate \( \nabla^2(r^4) \) at \( r = 1 \).

(A) 12
(B) 16
(C) 20
(D) 24
(E) 28
[/QUESTION]

Setting \( n = -1 \) gives the second radial example the topic calls for:
\[ \nabla^2\!\left(\frac{1}{r}\right) = (-1)(0)\,r^{-3} = 0, \qquad r \neq 0. \]
So \( 1/r \) has vanishing Laplacian everywhere except at the origin, where \( r=0 \) and the formula (built using \( \partial r/\partial x = x/r \)) breaks down since it divides by \( r \).

[QUESTION 4]
Using linearity together with \( \nabla^2(r^2) = 6 \) and \( \nabla^2(1/r) = 0 \) for \( r \neq 0 \), compute \( \nabla^2\!\left(3r^2 + \dfrac{2}{r}\right) \) at \( r = 2 \).

(A) 6
(B) 10
(C) 14
(D) 16
(E) 18
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 4: Polynomial Examples ===

Radial functions are not the only fields worth computing by hand. Consider \( f(x,y,z) = x^3 - 3xy^2 \), a field with no \( z \)-dependence at all. Its second partials:
\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 3x^2 - 3y^2, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = 6x, \]
\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -6xy, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} = -6x, \]
\[ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} = 0 \quad (\text{no } z \text{ dependence}). \]
Adding these,
\[ \nabla^2 f = 6x - 6x + 0 = 0 \]
at every point — the two curvatures in \( x \) and \( y \) cancel exactly, everywhere, not just at one point. This is a qualitatively different kind of result from \( \nabla^2(r^2)=6 \): a nontrivial, non-constant polynomial whose second-derivative sum is identically zero rather than some fixed nonzero number.

[QUESTION 5]
Let \( f(x,y,z) = x^2y^2 + yz^2 \). Compute \( \nabla^2 f \) at \( (1,2,3) \).

(A) 8
(B) 10
(C) 12
(D) 14
(E) 16
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 5: Harmonic Functions ===

The vanishing result for \( x^3-3xy^2 \) and for \( 1/r \) (away from the origin) are instances of the same phenomenon, and it is worth naming: a scalar field \( f \) is called harmonic on a region if \( \nabla^2 f = 0 \) at every point of that region. Physically, by the concavity reading built in Section 1, a harmonic field has no interior points that bulge above or dip below their immediate surroundings — its value at any point is, in a precise sense, perfectly balanced against its neighbors in every direction.

A few structural facts follow immediately from what has already been established. Constant functions and linear functions \( f = ax+by+cz+d \) are harmonic, since every second partial derivative of a degree-one polynomial is zero — no computation beyond that observation is needed. By linearity (Section 2), if \( f \) and \( g \) are both harmonic then so is \( af+bg \) for any constants \( a,b \), since \( \nabla^2(af+bg) = a\cdot 0 + b\cdot 0 = 0 \); the set of harmonic functions on a region is closed under linear combination. And \( 1/r \) is harmonic on any region not containing the origin, by the Section 3 computation.

[TABLE]
Function | \( \nabla^2 f \) | Harmonic?
\( r^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2 \) | 6 | No
\( 1/r \), \( r\neq 0 \) | 0 | Yes
\( x^3 - 3xy^2 \) | 0 | Yes
\( ax+by+cz+d \) | 0 | Yes
[/TABLE]

[QUESTION 6]
Which of the following functions is harmonic (satisfies \( \nabla^2 f = 0 \) everywhere it is defined)?

(A) \( f = x^2+y^2+z^2 \)
(B) \( f = x^2 - y^2 \)
(C) \( f = x^2 + xy \)
(D) \( f = xy^2 \)
(E) \( f = x^3 \)
[/QUESTION]

It is worth being precise about what "closed under linear combination" buys you and what it does not: it says nothing about combining a harmonic field with one that is not harmonic, since the non-harmonic piece contributes its own nonzero Laplacian to the sum, scaled by whatever constant multiplies it.

[QUESTION 7]
Suppose \( f \) is harmonic (\( \nabla^2 f = 0 \) everywhere) and \( g \) satisfies \( \nabla^2 g = 6 \) everywhere. For what value of the constant \( c \) does \( h = f + cg \) satisfy \( \nabla^2 h = 15 \) everywhere?

(A) 2
(B) 2.5
(C) 3
(D) 3.5
(E) 5
[/QUESTION]

=== SECTION 6: Laplace's Equation and the Heat Equation ===

Framed as a partial differential equation rather than a property of a given field, \( \nabla^2 f = 0 \) is called Laplace's equation, and a harmonic function is exactly a solution of it. This equation is where the opening problem's steady-state temperature actually connects to the Laplacian by name.

To see the connection, return to the physics. Fourier's law of heat conduction says heat flows down the temperature gradient, with flux vector \( \mathbf{J} = -k\nabla u \) for a scalar temperature field \( u \) and a positive conductivity \( k \); the minus sign encodes that heat moves from hot toward cold. Conservation of energy in a region with no internal sources says the rate at which heat accumulates at a point equals the negative of the net outflow there, i.e. \( \partial u/\partial t \) is proportional to \( -\nabla \cdot \mathbf{J} \). Substituting the flux law,
\[ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = -\nabla \cdot(-k\nabla u) = k\,\nabla\cdot(\nabla u) = k\nabla^2 u. \]
This is the heat equation, and it is precisely why the divergence-of-gradient construction from Section 1 is the operator that governs diffusion: the gradient supplies the flux direction via Fourier's law, and the divergence measures whether that flux is net accumulating or net escaping at each point. Setting \( \partial u/\partial t = 0 \) — the plate from the opening problem, no longer changing in time — collapses the heat equation exactly to Laplace's equation \( \nabla^2 u = 0 \), so a steady-state temperature distribution with no internal sources is precisely a harmonic function.

[QUESTION 8]
The heat equation is \( \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} = k\nabla^2 u \) with diffusivity \( k = 2 \). At a certain point and time, \( \nabla^2 u = 7 \). What is \( \partial u/\partial t \) there at that instant?

(A) 3.5
(B) 7
(C) 9
(D) 12
(E) 14
[/QUESTION]

This also finally answers the opening problem in full, away from the idealized steady state. If a point is not yet in equilibrium and \( \nabla^2 u < 0 \) there, Section 1's reading says the gradient field is collapsing inward at that point, which happens exactly when \( u \) bulges above its immediate surroundings — the point is hotter than the local average. By Fourier's law, heat then flows away from that point in every direction, and the heat equation says \( \partial u/\partial t = k\nabla^2 u \) is negative there too, so the temperature at that point falls over time, relaxing it back toward its neighbors.

[QUESTION 9]
In a heat-conducting medium (not necessarily at steady state) with \( \partial u/\partial t = k\nabla^2 u \), \( k>0 \), suppose at some point \( \nabla^2 u < 0 \). Fourier's law says the heat flux is \( -k\nabla u \), directed from hot toward cold. What does the sign of \( \nabla^2 u \) tell you about that point relative to its immediate surroundings, and how is the temperature there changing in time?

(A) It is colder than its surroundings on average; temperature there is increasing
(B) It is hotter than its surroundings on average; temperature there is decreasing
(C) It is hotter than its surroundings on average; temperature there is increasing
(D) It is colder than its surroundings on average; temperature there is decreasing
(E) No relation can be determined from this information
[/QUESTION]

[KEY: 1D 2E 3C 4E 5D 6B 7B 8E 9B]

[BONUS 1]
[ANSWER: C]
The Laplacian obeys a product rule, \( \nabla^2(fg) = f\nabla^2 g + g\nabla^2 f + 2\nabla f \cdot \nabla g \), which follows from the divergence product rule \( \nabla\cdot(h\mathbf{F}) = h\,\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F} + \nabla h \cdot \mathbf{F} \) (itself a consequence of the ordinary product rule applied to each component) applied with \( h=f \), \( \mathbf{F} = \nabla g \), and then symmetrized in \( f \) and \( g \). Let \( f = xyz \) (for which \( \nabla^2 f = 0 \), since each second partial derivative of \( xyz \) with respect to the same variable twice is zero) and \( g = r^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2 \) (for which \( \nabla^2 g = 6 \)). Compute \( \nabla^2(fg) \) at \( (1,1,1) \).

(A) 12
(B) 15
(C) 18
(D) 21
(E) 24
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 2]
[ANSWER: D]
Using \( \nabla^2(r^n) = n(n+1)\,r^{n-2} \) for \( r \neq 0 \), for which values of \( n \) is \( r^n \) harmonic away from the origin?

(A) \( n=0 \) only
(B) \( n=-1 \) only
(C) \( n=0 \) and \( n=1 \)
(D) \( n=0 \) and \( n=-1 \)
(E) \( n=1 \) and \( n=-1 \)
[/BONUS]

[BONUS 3]
[ANSWER: C]
A steady-state temperature field with a uniform internal heat source no longer satisfies Laplace's equation but instead \( \nabla^2 u = -Q/k \) for a constant \( Q/k \), since the source term breaks the zero-net-flow balance used to derive \( \nabla^2 u = 0 \) in Section 6. Suppose \( u(x,y,z) = A\,r^2 \) for a constant \( A \), and \( Q/k = 12 \). Using \( \nabla^2(r^2) = 6 \) and linearity, find \( A \).

(A) -4
(B) -3
(C) -2
(D) -1
(E) 2
[/BONUS]

nodes.label: Curl of a Gradient and Divergence of a Curl
nodes.explanation: Covers the two identically-zero second-derivative identities, ∇×(∇f)=0 and ∇·(∇×A)=0, their short proofs via equality of mixed partial derivatives, and their standard significance: why curl-free fields are (at least locally) gradients and divergence-free fields are (at least locally) curls, including a brief, non-rigorous mention of the topological caveat (simply-connected domains) with a counterexample. Does not attempt a full existence proof of potentials (that needs integral/topological tools outside this tree) and does not cover curl-of-curl, which is a separate, much harder identity handled elsewhere.

nodes.label: Product Rule Identities for Scalar–Vector Products
nodes.explanation: Covers the three del-operator product rules where one factor is a scalar field: ∇(fg)=f∇g+g∇f, ∇·(fA)=f(∇·A)+A·∇f, and ∇×(fA)=f(∇×A)−A×∇f, each derived by direct Cartesian component expansion and illustrated with physical examples (e.g. the continuity-equation form ∇·(ρv)). Does not cover identities combining two independent vector fields (∇(A·B), ∇·(A×B), ∇×(A×B)), which need a genuinely different derivation technique and belong to a separate node.

nodes.label: Index Notation for Vector Calculus
nodes.explanation: Introduces Einstein summation convention, the Kronecker delta δ_ij, the Levi-Civita symbol ε_ijk and its antisymmetry/cyclic properties, and how to rewrite dot products, cross products, gradient, divergence, and curl in index form. This is purely the notational toolkit; it stops short of the epsilon-delta contraction identity and its use in deriving specific vector identities, which is the next node.

nodes.label: The Epsilon–Delta (Contraction) Identity
nodes.explanation: Covers the identity ε_ijkε_ilm=δ_jlδ_km−δ_jmδ_kl, its proof, the related fully-contracted result ε_ijkε_ijk=6, and the general strategy of using it to collapse a product of two Levi-Civita symbols into Kronecker deltas, demonstrated on the ordinary (del-free) vector triple product a×(b×c) as a worked warm-up. Does not apply the technique to any specific del-operator identity (curl-of-curl, ∇(A·B), ∇×(A×B)) — those applications are each handled in their own downstream nodes.

nodes.label: Product Rule Identities for Two Vector Fields
nodes.explanation: Covers the three del-operator identities that combine two independent vector fields A and B: ∇(A·B)=(A·∇)B+(B·∇)A+A×(∇×B)+B×(∇×A), ∇·(A×B)=B·(∇×A)−A·(∇×B), and ∇×(A×B)=(B·∇)A−(A·∇)B+A(∇·B)−B(∇·A), including the definition of the directional/convective derivative operator (A·∇) needed to state them. Derivations lean on the epsilon-delta contraction identity for the two harder cases (∇(A·B) and ∇×(A×B)); does not cover the scalar-vector product rules (a separate node) or the curl-of-curl identity, which involves the same field twice and is treated on its own.

nodes.label: Curl of the Curl and the Vector Laplacian
nodes.explanation: Derives ∇×(∇×A)=∇(∇·A)−∇²A using the epsilon-delta identity, and uses this relation to define the vector Laplacian ∇²A in general coordinates, contrasting it with the naive (Cartesian-only) componentwise definition. Includes worked examples and the classic application to deriving the electromagnetic wave equation from ∇×(∇×E). Does not cover the two-vector-field product rules (different derivation target) or the Helmholtz decomposition, which builds on this result.

nodes.label: Helmholtz Decomposition Theorem
nodes.explanation: States the Helmholtz decomposition F=−∇φ+∇×A for a sufficiently well-behaved vector field, explains why the identically-zero identities guarantee the −∇φ part is curl-free and the ∇×A part is divergence-free, and sketches how taking the divergence and curl of F together with the curl-of-curl/vector-Laplacian identity leads to Poisson-type equations ∇²φ=−∇·F and ∇²A=−∇×F for constructing φ and A. Presented at the level of statement and plausibility construction rather than a full rigorous existence/uniqueness proof, which would require boundary-condition and Green's-function machinery outside this tree's scope.

nodes.label: The Laplacian of 1/r and the Dirac Delta Function
nodes.explanation: Enrichment node covering the distributional identity ∇²(1/r)=−4πδ³(r): it reconciles the pointwise result ∇²(1/r)=0 for r≠0 (already seen as an example in the scalar Laplacian node) with the nonzero total behavior at the origin, motivated conceptually rather than via a full rigorous divergence-theorem proof. Included for its importance in electrostatics (Poisson's equation for a point charge) but not load-bearing for any other node in this tree.
